name: Statistics
description: Introductory statistics covering data collection, descriptive statistics, probability, distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, regression, and real-world data analysis.

modules.title: Introduction to Data
modules.objectives: Distinguish between categorical and quantitative data; compare observational studies and experiments; identify sampling methods (simple random, stratified, cluster, systematic); recognize sources of bias.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Introductory Statistics — Sections 1.1-1.4: definitions, data, sampling, experiments, and observational studies.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — open Statistics, Module 1: Introduction to Data, and complete the listed lesson before the single-attempt quiz.
modules.practiceNote: Complete the ungraded practice embedded in Statistics, Module 1: Introduction to Data; use the assignment above for the required teacher-reviewed work.
modules.assignment: Use this GIIS-authored study vignette: A school randomly chooses 4 of its 20 homerooms and surveys every student in those rooms about weekly sleep; 146 of 160 selected students respond. The survey finds an association between reported sleep and reported concentration. Classify the population, sample, variables, sampling method, nonresponse risk, study type, and the strongest justified conclusion. Submit: paste your numbered response into the assignment field. Include: explain why each classification fits the evidence, quote the relevant vignette fact, identify two limits, and rewrite an unjustified causal headline. Evaluation: classifications 40%; evidence and reasoning 35%; limitations and claim wording 25%. Submission alone does not demonstrate mastery.

modules.title: Displaying Data
modules.objectives: Construct and interpret bar graphs, histograms, box plots, stem-and-leaf plots, and dot plots; choose the most appropriate display for a given data set.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Introductory Statistics — Sections 2.1-2.4: frequency tables, histograms, frequency polygons, and box plots.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — open Statistics, Module 2: Displaying Data, and complete the listed lesson before the single-attempt quiz.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Statistics #6 — Data Visualization Part 2.
modules.practiceNote: Complete the ungraded practice embedded in Statistics, Module 2: Displaying Data; use the assignment above for the required teacher-reviewed work.
modules.assignment: Use the synthetic commute-time dataset in minutes: 12,15,18,18,20,22,24,25,27,30,31,35,38,42,45,50,55,60,70,95. Create a frequency table with bins 0-19,20-39,40-59,60-79,80-99; draw a histogram, dot plot, and modified box plot; then compare what each display reveals about shape, center, spread, and possible outliers. Submit: paste your numbered response or a teacher-accessible link. Include: labeled axes and units, bin choices, five-number summary, stated quartile convention, 1.5-IQR fences, and evidence for every interpretation. Evaluation: displays 40%; calculations 30%; evidence-based comparison 30%. Submission alone does not demonstrate mastery.

modules.title: Descriptive Statistics: Center & Spread
modules.objectives: Calculate mean, median, and mode; compute range, IQR, variance, and standard deviation; identify outliers using the 1.5×IQR rule. Students will show step-by-step reasoning, check solutions for accuracy, and apply the method to the module assignment or a real problem.

modules.assignment: Use the synthetic scores 40, 68, 70, 72, 74, 75, 76, 78, 80, 82, 84, 86, 88, 90, 92. Compute the mean, median, sample variance and sample standard deviation. Find Q1 and Q3 by excluding the overall median, calculate 1.5-IQR fences, identify flagged values, then recompute summaries without each flagged value and explain whether removal is justified. Submit: paste your numbered response into the assignment field, or provide a teacher-accessible link to a legible document or diagram. Include: explain why each selected method fits the problem and cite calculation or scientific evidence for each conclusion; all calculations, the n-1 convention, quartiles, fences, before/after summaries, and an evidence-based decision about any flagged value. Evaluation: numerical accuracy 50%; method and notation 30%; interpretation of outliers 20%. Submission alone does not demonstrate mastery.

questions.question: A researcher surveys every 10th person on a voter registration list. This is an example of which sampling method?
questions.explanation: Systematic sampling selects every kth element from a list after a random start.

questions.question: Which of the following is a categorical variable?
questions.explanation: Categorical variables represent groups or labels, not numerical measurements. It connects the correct answer to Statistics midterm concepts and separates it from plausible distractors.

questions.question: A histogram is most appropriate for displaying which type of data?
options: Categorical data with a few categories
questions.explanation: Histograms group continuous numerical values into bins and display their frequencies.

questions.question: What is the interquartile range (IQR) of the data set {3, 5, 7, 8, 12, 15, 20}?
questions.explanation: Q1 is 5 and Q3 is 15, so the IQR is 15 - 5 = 10. This reinforces the Statistics midterm concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: A data set has mean 70 and standard deviation 5. A score of 80 has a z-score of:
questions.explanation: z = (80 − 70) / 5 = 10 / 5 = 2. Students need to recognize why 2 matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

questions.question: According to the empirical rule, approximately what percentage of data falls within two standard deviations of the mean in a normal distribution?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule states 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD.

questions.question: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue marbles. If one marble is drawn at random, what is the probability it is red?
questions.explanation: Four of ten equally likely marbles are red, so 4/10 = 2/5. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

questions.question: Events A and B are mutually exclusive. If P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4, what is P(A or B)?
questions.explanation: For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.70. The reasoning points back to the procedure used in Statistics midterm concepts, which helps students check the calculation rather than guess from the options.

questions.question: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A and B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent?
options: Yes, because P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B)
No, because P(A and B) ≠ P(A)·P(B)
Yes, because they are mutually exclusive
questions.answer: Yes, because P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B)
questions.explanation: P(A)·P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 = P(A and B), so A and B are independent. This reinforces the Statistics midterm concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: A binomial experiment has n = 8 and p = 0.5. What is the expected number of successes?
questions.explanation: Expected value of a binomial: E(X) = np = 8 × 0.5 = 4. It highlights the operation, property, or model that makes the answer work in Statistics midterm concepts.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a condition for a binomial distribution?
options: Probability of success changes each trial
Only two possible outcomes per trial
questions.answer: Probability of success changes each trial
questions.explanation: A binomial distribution requires a constant probability of success across all trials.

questions.question: Four independent fair coin flips are made. What is the probability of exactly three heads?
questions.explanation: There are C(4,3)=4 such outcomes, each with probability (1/2)^4, so the probability is 4/16 = 1/4. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

questions.question: X has a binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.20. What is Var(X)?
questions.explanation: Var(X)=np(1-p)=10(0.20)(0.80)=1.6. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

questions.question: A fair spinner has five equal sections numbered 1-5. Which gives its sample space, P(odd), and P(number > 3)?
questions.explanation: Odd outcomes are 1, 3, and 5; outcomes greater than 3 are 4 and 5. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

questions.question: For ages 24, 28, 31, 35, 35, 40, and 52, what are the mean and median?
questions.explanation: The sum is 245, so the mean is 245/7=35; the fourth ordered value is 35. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

questions.question: In an observational study, what does the researcher do?
options: Randomly assigns every participant to a control group
questions.explanation: In an observational study, the researcher observes existing conditions and does not impose treatments.

questions.question: Which display is best for showing the distribution shape of a large quantitative data set?
questions.explanation: Histograms reveal shape, center, and spread of large quantitative data sets through frequency bins.

questions.question: A distribution is right-skewed. Which statement is generally true?
questions.explanation: In a right-skewed distribution, the tail pulls the mean to the right, making it larger than the median.

questions.question: A data value is an outlier by the 1.5×IQR rule if it is below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above:
questions.explanation: The upper fence is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Values above this fence are considered outliers.

questions.question: A student scores at the 84th percentile on a normally distributed exam with mean 70 and standard deviation 10. Approximately what is the student's score?
questions.explanation: The 84th percentile is about one standard deviation above the mean, so the score is approximately 70 + 10 = 80.

questions.question: If P(A) = 0.6 and A and B are independent with P(B) = 0.3, what is P(A and B)?
questions.explanation: Independence gives P(A and B)=P(A)P(B)=0.6(0.3)=0.18. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

questions.question: P(B|A) = 0.4, P(A) = 0.5. What is P(A and B)?
questions.explanation: Multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(B|A) × P(A) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.20. The choice fits the prompt because it applies the central rule or concept from Statistics final concepts.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has E(X) = 3 and E(X²) = 13. What is Var(X)?
questions.explanation: Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = 13 − 9 = 4. It highlights the operation, property, or model that makes the answer work in Statistics final concepts.

questions.question: As sample size increases, what happens to the standard error of the mean?
questions.explanation: The standard error is σ/√n, so increasing n makes the standard error smaller.

questions.question: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is (48, 56). Which interpretation is correct?
options: The population mean is 52 with probability 0.95
95% of all data values lie between 48 and 56
We are 95% confident the true population mean lies between 48 and 56
5% of sample means fall outside this interval
questions.answer: We are 95% confident the true population mean lies between 48 and 56
questions.explanation: A confidence interval means we used a method that captures the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples.

questions.question: Which of the following increases the margin of error of a confidence interval for a mean?
questions.explanation: Margin of error = z* × (σ/√n). A larger σ directly increases the margin of error.

questions.question: In a hypothesis test, the p-value is 0.03 and α = 0.05. The correct decision is to:
questions.explanation: Since p = 0.03 < α = 0.05, the result is statistically significant and we reject the null hypothesis.

questions.question: Which situation describes a Type II error?
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Failing to reject a true null hypothesis
questions.answer: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
questions.explanation: A Type II error occurs when the null hypothesis is false, but the test fails to reject it.

questions.question: A chi-square goodness-of-fit test is used to determine whether:
options: Observed frequencies match expected frequencies for one variable
A population proportion equals a claimed value
questions.answer: Observed frequencies match expected frequencies for one variable
questions.explanation: The goodness-of-fit test compares observed counts in categories to theoretically expected counts.

questions.question: If the correlation coefficient r = −0.85, which statement best describes the relationship?
questions.explanation: r close to −1 indicates a strong negative linear association between the two variables.

questions.question: For the regression line ŷ = 3.2x + 10, what does the slope 3.2 represent?
options: The predicted increase in y for each one-unit increase in x
The residual for the mean x-value
questions.answer: The predicted increase in y for each one-unit increase in x
questions.explanation: The slope is the rate of change: for each 1-unit increase in x, y is predicted to increase by 3.2.

questions.question: If r² = 0.64 for a regression model predicting y from x, which statement is correct?
options: 64% of the variation in y is explained by x
64% of the variation in x is explained by y
The slope of the regression line is 0.64
questions.answer: 64% of the variation in y is explained by x
questions.explanation: The coefficient of determination describes the proportion of variation in the response variable y explained by the predictor x.

questions.question: A pollster samples 1,000 voters and finds 58% support a policy. The margin of error at 95% confidence is ±3%. Which statement is valid?
options: 58% of all voters support the policy
We are certain the true proportion is between 55% and 61%
We are 95% confident the true proportion is between 55% and 61%
The sample size is too small to draw any conclusion
questions.answer: We are 95% confident the true proportion is between 55% and 61%
questions.explanation: The confidence interval is 58% ± 3% = (55%, 61%). We interpret it as 95% confidence, not certainty.

questions.question: A graph that starts its y-axis at 50 instead of 0 to exaggerate differences between bars is an example of:
questions.explanation: Truncating the y-axis makes small differences appear much larger, misleading the viewer.

questions.question: A study finds r=0.91 between monthly ice cream sales and drowning rates. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The association alone does not establish causation; season could affect both variables
The correlation proves ice cream causes drowning
A correlation of 0.91 means 91% of drownings are caused by ice cream
Positive correlation rules out lurking variables
questions.answer: The association alone does not establish causation; season could affect both variables
questions.explanation: Correlation alone cannot establish causation. Season is a plausible lurking variable, but this association does not demonstrate the cause. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a quantitative variable?
quizQuestions.explanation: Height is a numerical measurement that can be compared and computed — a quantitative variable.

quizQuestions.question: An experiment differs from an observational study because it:
quizQuestions.explanation: In an experiment, the researcher actively imposes a treatment and measures the response.

quizQuestions.question: Which sampling method gives every possible sample of n distinct population members the same probability of selection?
quizQuestions.explanation: A simple random sample gives every possible sample of the stated size an equal chance. Equal individual inclusion probabilities alone would not uniquely identify this design.

quizQuestions.question: Which listed variable is quantitative rather than categorical?
quizQuestions.explanation: Height in inches is numerical and can be measured, so it is quantitative. The reasoning points back to the procedure used in Introduction to Data, which helps students check the calculation rather than guess from the options.

quizQuestions.question: A box plot displays which five summary statistics?
quizQuestions.explanation: The five-number summary shown in a box plot: minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum.

quizQuestions.question: A histogram with a long tail to the right is described as:
quizQuestions.explanation: A right (positive) skew means the longer tail extends toward higher values on the right.

quizQuestions.question: Which graph is best for comparing the distribution of a numerical variable across two groups?
quizQuestions.explanation: Side-by-side box plots allow visual comparison of center, spread, and skew across groups.

quizQuestions.question: In a stem-and-leaf plot for the value 37, the stem is:
quizQuestions.explanation: In a stem-and-leaf plot, the tens digit (3) is the stem and the units digit (7) is the leaf.

quizQuestions.question: Which five-number summary is displayed by a box plot?
options: Mean, median, mode, range, standard deviation
quizQuestions.explanation: A box plot displays the minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum.

quizQuestions.question: Which measure of center is most affected by outliers?
quizQuestions.explanation: The mean uses all data values in its calculation, so extreme values (outliers) pull it strongly.

quizQuestions.question: Find the median of: 4, 7, 9, 12, 15.
quizQuestions.explanation: Sorted list: 4, 7, 9, 12, 15. The middle value (3rd of 5) is 9. It connects the correct answer to Descriptive Statistics: Center & Spread and separates it from plausible distractors.

quizQuestions.question: In Descriptive Statistics: Center & Spread, The IQR is defined as:
quizQuestions.explanation: IQR (Interquartile Range) = Q3 − Q1, representing the spread of the middle 50% of data.

quizQuestions.question: Which measure of center changes the most when an outlier is added?
quizQuestions.explanation: The mean uses every value, so extreme values can pull it upward or downward.

quizQuestions.question: What is the median of the data set 4, 7, 9, 12, 15?
quizQuestions.explanation: The values are already ordered, and the middle value is 9. It highlights the operation, property, or model that makes the answer work in Descriptive Statistics: Center & Spread.

quizQuestions.question: What shape does a normal distribution have?
quizQuestions.explanation: The normal distribution is perfectly symmetric around its mean and bell-shaped.

quizQuestions.question: A test score of 85 has a z-score of 1.0. The mean is 75. What is the standard deviation?
quizQuestions.explanation: z = (x − μ)/σ → 1.0 = (85 − 75)/σ → σ = 10/1.0 = 10. It highlights the operation, property, or model that makes the answer work in Normal Distribution.

quizQuestions.question: In a normal distribution with mean 100 and SD 15, what percentage of values lie between 85 and 115?
quizQuestions.explanation: 85 and 115 are each 1 SD from the mean (100 ± 15). The empirical rule states 68% of data lies within 1 SD.

quizQuestions.question: A z-score of −2 means the value is:
quizQuestions.explanation: Negative z-scores indicate the value is below the mean. z = −2 means 2 SDs below.

quizQuestions.question: For a standard normal variable Z, approximately what is P(Z < 1.96)?
quizQuestions.explanation: Approximately 95% lies between -1.96 and 1.96, leaving 2.5% above 1.96. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

quizQuestions.question: When flipping a fair coin, what is the probability of getting heads?
quizQuestions.explanation: A fair coin has two equally likely outcomes: heads and tails. P(heads) = 1/2 = 0.5.

quizQuestions.question: Two events are mutually exclusive if:
options: They cannot both occur at the same time
quizQuestions.answer: They cannot both occur at the same time
quizQuestions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common; P(A and B) = 0. This reinforces the Probability Fundamentals idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

quizQuestions.question: P(A) = 0.7. What is P(not A)?
quizQuestions.explanation: Complement rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3. It connects the correct answer to Probability Fundamentals and separates it from plausible distractors.

quizQuestions.question: A single card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is P(drawing a king or a heart)?
quizQuestions.explanation: P(king) = 4/52, P(heart) = 13/52, P(king and heart) = 1/52. P(king or heart) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52.

quizQuestions.question: The sum of all probabilities in a valid probability distribution must equal:
quizQuestions.explanation: A valid probability distribution requires that all probabilities are non-negative and sum to exactly 1.

quizQuestions.question: For one flip of a fair coin, what is P(heads)?
quizQuestions.explanation: A fair coin has two equally likely outcomes, so P(heads) = 1/2 = 0.5. The reasoning points back to the procedure used in Probability Fundamentals, which helps students check the calculation rather than guess from the options.

quizQuestions.question: In Conditional Probability & Independence, P(A|B) is read as:
options: The probability of A and B
The probability of A given B
The probability of B given A
The probability of A or B
quizQuestions.answer: The probability of A given B
quizQuestions.explanation: Conditional probability P(A|B) means the probability of event A occurring, given that B has already occurred.

quizQuestions.question: If P(A and B) = 0.12, P(B) = 0.4, what is P(A|B)?
quizQuestions.explanation: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B) = 0.12 / 0.4 = 0.30. It highlights the operation, property, or model that makes the answer work in Conditional Probability & Independence.

quizQuestions.question: Two events are independent if:
quizQuestions.explanation: Independence means knowing B occurred does not change the probability of A: P(A|B) = P(A).

quizQuestions.question: In Conditional Probability & Independence, how is P(A|B) read?
options: The probability of A and B
The probability of A given B
The probability of B given A
The probability of A or B
quizQuestions.answer: The probability of A given B
quizQuestions.explanation: The vertical bar means "given," so P(A|B) is read as the probability of A given B.

quizQuestions.question: Of 100 students, 40 take art, 30 take music, and 12 take both. What is P(art | music)?
quizQuestions.explanation: Restrict the denominator to the 30 music students: 12/30=0.40. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

quizQuestions.question: For a discrete probability distribution, all probabilities must be:
options: Between 0 and 1 inclusive, and sum to 1
quizQuestions.answer: Between 0 and 1 inclusive, and sum to 1
quizQuestions.explanation: Valid probabilities are non-negative, at most 1, and all possible outcome probabilities sum to 1.

quizQuestions.question: Which scenario is a binomial setting?
options: Drawing cards without replacement from a deck
Rolling a die until a 6 appears
Flipping a coin 20 times and counting heads
quizQuestions.answer: Flipping a coin 20 times and counting heads
quizQuestions.explanation: Fixed n = 20, two outcomes (H/T), constant probability, independent trials — all binomial conditions are met.

quizQuestions.question: The formula for binomial probability P(X = k) is:
quizQuestions.explanation: The binomial formula multiplies the combination C(n,k) by the probability of exactly k successes and (n−k) failures.

quizQuestions.question: For a discrete probability distribution, what must be true of all probabilities?
options: They must be between 0 and 1 inclusive and sum to 1
They must sum to the sample size
quizQuestions.answer: They must be between 0 and 1 inclusive and sum to 1
quizQuestions.explanation: Valid probabilities cannot be below 0 or above 1, and the probabilities of all outcomes must total 1.

quizQuestions.question: For independent, identically distributed observations from a population with finite mean and finite positive variance, what does the Central Limit Theorem imply as n becomes large?
options: The standardized sample mean approaches a standard normal distribution
quizQuestions.answer: The standardized sample mean approaches a standard normal distribution
quizQuestions.explanation: The theorem concerns the standardized sample mean. A finite-sample approximation depends on population shape, so 30 is not a universal guarantee.

quizQuestions.question: The standard error of the sample mean equals:
quizQuestions.explanation: Standard error of the mean = σ/√n, measuring how much the sample mean varies from sample to sample.

quizQuestions.question: A population has μ = 40 and σ = 8. For n = 16, what is the mean of the sampling distribution of x̄?
quizQuestions.explanation: The mean of the sampling distribution of x̄ always equals the population mean μ = 40.

quizQuestions.question: Increasing sample size from n = 25 to n = 100 reduces the standard error by a factor of:
quizQuestions.explanation: SE = σ/√n. √100/√25 = 10/5 = 2. So the SE is halved — reduced by a factor of 2.

quizQuestions.question: When is the Central Limit Theorem commonly used for a sample mean?
options: When n ≥ 30 or the population is normal
Only when the population is uniform
When the sample has no variation
quizQuestions.answer: When n ≥ 30 or the population is normal
quizQuestions.explanation: A large sample size, often n ≥ 30, or a normal population supports using the normal model for the sample mean.

quizQuestions.question: When should you use a t-distribution instead of z for a confidence interval for a mean?
options: When population standard deviation is unknown
quizQuestions.answer: When population standard deviation is unknown
quizQuestions.explanation: The t-distribution is used when σ is unknown and s (sample SD) is used instead.

quizQuestions.question: Degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-interval with n = 20 is:
quizQuestions.explanation: Degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-procedure: df = n − 1 = 20 − 1 = 19. It highlights the operation, property, or model that makes the answer work in Confidence Intervals: Means.

quizQuestions.question: A 99% confidence interval is _________ than a 95% confidence interval from the same data.
quizQuestions.explanation: Higher confidence requires a larger critical value, which increases the margin of error and widens the interval.

quizQuestions.question: When should a t-distribution be used instead of z for a confidence interval for a mean?
options: When the population standard deviation is unknown
When the sample size is exactly 100
quizQuestions.answer: When the population standard deviation is unknown
quizQuestions.explanation: The t-distribution is used for a mean when the population standard deviation is unknown and must be estimated from the sample.

quizQuestions.question: What are the degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-interval with n = 20?
quizQuestions.explanation: For a one-sample t-interval, degrees of freedom are n - 1, so 20 - 1 = 19. This reinforces the Confidence Intervals: Means idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

quizQuestions.question: The formula for the margin of error of a proportion confidence interval is:
quizQuestions.explanation: Margin of error for a proportion: ME = z* × √(p̂(1−p̂)/n). This reinforces the Confidence Intervals: Proportions idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

quizQuestions.question: In a sample of 200, 80 said yes. What is the sample proportion p̂?
quizQuestions.explanation: p̂ = 80/200 = 0.40. The reasoning points back to the procedure used in Confidence Intervals: Proportions, which helps students check the calculation rather than guess from the options.

quizQuestions.question: To reduce the margin of error by half, you must multiply the sample size by:
quizQuestions.explanation: ME ∝ 1/√n. To halve ME, you need √n to double, so n must be multiplied by 4.

quizQuestions.question: When no prior estimate of p is available, which value is used to conservatively calculate required sample size?
quizQuestions.explanation: p = 0.5 maximizes p(1−p), giving the largest (most conservative) required sample size.

quizQuestions.question: A symmetric one-proportion z-interval is (0.42, 0.58). What is its point estimate?
quizQuestions.explanation: The point estimate is the interval midpoint: (0.42+0.58)/2=0.50. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

quizQuestions.question: Using p=0.50 and z*=1.96, what minimum sample size gives a planned margin of error no greater than 0.05?
quizQuestions.explanation: n must be at least 1.96^2(0.5)(0.5)/0.05^2=384.16, so round upward to 385. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

quizQuestions.question: The null hypothesis (H₀) typically states:
options: There is no effect or no difference
quizQuestions.answer: There is no effect or no difference
quizQuestions.explanation: The null hypothesis is the default assumption of no effect, no difference, or a specific claimed value.

quizQuestions.question: A p-value of 0.001 at α = 0.05 means:
options: Reject H₀; strong evidence against it
quizQuestions.answer: Reject H₀; strong evidence against it
quizQuestions.explanation: p = 0.001 < 0.05 = α. We reject H₀; the extremely small p-value suggests strong evidence against the null.

quizQuestions.question: In Hypothesis Testing: Means, A Type I error is:
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
quizQuestions.explanation: Type I error (α): incorrectly rejecting H₀ when it is actually true — a false positive.

quizQuestions.question: The t-test statistic for a one-sample test is computed as:
quizQuestions.explanation: The one-sample t-statistic uses the sample SD (s) since population σ is unknown.

quizQuestions.question: A two-tailed test with α = 0.05 splits the rejection region into:
quizQuestions.explanation: For a two-tailed test, the significance level α is split equally: α/2 = 0.025 in each tail.

quizQuestions.question: What does the null hypothesis H₀ typically state?
options: There is no effect or no difference
The sample mean is always zero
The p-value is always below alpha
quizQuestions.answer: There is no effect or no difference
quizQuestions.explanation: The null hypothesis usually represents the default claim of no effect, no difference, or no change.

quizQuestions.question: The chi-square statistic is calculated as:
quizQuestions.explanation: Chi-square: χ² = Σ(Observed − Expected)² / Expected, summed over all categories.

quizQuestions.question: Degrees of freedom for a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with 5 categories is:
quizQuestions.explanation: df = number of categories − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4. The reasoning points back to the procedure used in Hypothesis Testing: Proportions & Chi-Square, which helps students check the calculation rather than guess from the options.

quizQuestions.question: A chi-square test of independence tests whether:
options: Two categorical variables are associated in a population
Observed proportions match a claimed value
A single mean equals a null value
quizQuestions.answer: Two categorical variables are associated in a population
quizQuestions.explanation: The chi-square test of independence examines whether two categorical variables are related or independent.

quizQuestions.question: What formula is used to calculate the chi-square statistic?
quizQuestions.explanation: The chi-square statistic sums (observed minus expected) squared, divided by expected, across categories.

quizQuestions.question: For a one-proportion z-test with p0=0.50, n=100, and p-hat=0.58, what is z?
quizQuestions.explanation: z=(0.58-0.50)/sqrt(0.50(0.50)/100)=1.60. This calculation or biological mechanism directly supports the keyed option and rules out the alternatives under the conditions stated in the question.

quizQuestions.question: Which value of r indicates the strongest linear relationship?
quizQuestions.explanation: The strength of correlation is measured by |r|. |−0.85| = 0.85 is the largest among the options.

quizQuestions.question: In the regression equation ŷ = 2x + 5, what is the predicted y when x = 3?
quizQuestions.explanation: ŷ = 2(3) + 5 = 6 + 5 = 11. It highlights the operation, property, or model that makes the answer work in Linear Regression.

quizQuestions.question: In Linear Regression, A residual is defined as:
quizQuestions.explanation: Residual = actual observed value minus the predicted value from the regression line.

quizQuestions.question: Which correlation value indicates the strongest linear relationship?
quizQuestions.explanation: Strength depends on the absolute value of r; |−0.85| is the largest of the choices.

quizQuestions.question: A graph that uses 3D effects to exaggerate differences in a pie chart is an example of:
quizQuestions.explanation: 3D effects distort the relative sizes of pie slices, making some appear larger than they actually are.

quizQuestions.question: Correlation between ice cream sales and drowning rates is high. This means:
options: A lurking variable (e.g., hot weather) may explain both
quizQuestions.answer: A lurking variable (e.g., hot weather) may explain both
quizQuestions.explanation: Season or hot weather could influence both variables, so it is a plausible lurking variable. The reported association alone does not identify the cause or establish a causal effect.

quizQuestions.question: Data privacy in statistics means researchers must:
options: Protect the identities and sensitive information of participants
Share raw data with all readers
quizQuestions.answer: Protect the identities and sensitive information of participants
quizQuestions.explanation: Ethical research protects participant confidentiality, often through anonymization and informed consent.

quizQuestions.question: A study reports 'the drug reduced symptoms by 50%.' To evaluate this claim, you should ask:
options: What is the sample size and control group?
What country was the study in?
quizQuestions.answer: What is the sample size and control group?
quizQuestions.explanation: Evaluating statistical claims requires knowing the study design: sample size, control group, randomization, and confounders.

quizQuestions.question: A graph that uses 3D effects to exaggerate differences in a pie chart is an example of what?
quizQuestions.explanation: 3D effects can distort visual comparisons, making the graph misleading. This reinforces the Statistical Ethics & Real-World Applications idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.
